title: Hypertrophy Q&A #8
summary: Hypertrophy Q&A covering finishers, how evolving rep ranges and top sets drive progression, range of motion for novices, squat and deadlift variation pairing, delt and leg frequency, and injury and heat management. He dismisses mTOR resets and the scale-back-10% approach as powerlifting habits, and explains his aesthetic choices about shoulders, upper chest and legs.
claims: Finishers are fine as long as they complete hard sets rather than replace them, and target a muscle already pre-fatigued that session
He rarely does more than two or three finishers per session and picks the muscles he wants to completely exhaust that day
Trap finisher: shrug a weight you can do for about 15 reps, then pyramid down; he only drops weight between sets for finishers and keeps loads static otherwise
Finishers give pump and feel but do not replace mechanical tension
Do not use loaded barbell compounds as finishers; replicate them with bands, like banded overhead press for shoulders, or bodyweight hyperextensions for the hip hinge
He dislikes AMRAP sets for strength work and accessories because true AMRAPs get riskier as intensity rises; he only allows them for finishers and unweighted calisthenics
With an evolving rep range you already know how many reps you should hit; start conservative on a new lift and climb until the reps start to slow, which is when the numbers begin to matter
He runs evolving rep ranges with one rep in reserve because his strong lower back lets him grind squats and deadlifts and he does not want to
The first top set of an evolving rep range decides progression; the following sets with the same weight are volume for high-quality tonnage
When you hit the top of the range, add weight and drop to a holding rep range, for example 6 reps with 100 lb becomes 3 reps with 110 lb
Progressing by sets at fixed reps (2x6 to 4x6) builds tonnage but keeps intensity static and makes weight jumps hard; fine if you still add weight
Novices should use the range of motion they are comfortable with and keep working toward more; do not demand ass-to-grass squats before mobility allows
He squats heavy only to parallel but does front squat warm-ups and all pause squat reps ass-to-grass, which still gives him the benefits of full range
Partials reduce total muscle activation; the odd-lift partial craze produced guys who stayed small because they never built a base; partials are earned
If you bench five times a week, use variations that spare the shoulders or you are heading for injury
His favourite static rep ranges are 3x3 and 3x5, plus 1x5 for deadlifts; he likes 5x5 less but accepts it for back-off sets, knowing 25 reps is a lot of tonnage
Use one to three work sets, and usually two to three back-off sets
RPE is a valid intensity tool; he works the other way, using the rep range from experience to set intensity, and warns against training like a powerlifter for peak strength instead of tonnage
If you repeat 10 reps after 3 minutes of rest across four sets with no drop, the weight is too light and you did not fatigue the muscle; add weight
The same set can be junk volume when fresh but high intensity at the end of a hard workout; 10 reps at 225 lb squat is easy as an opener and brutal after squats, RDLs and front squats
Do your scheduled giant set even after deadlifts tire you out; deadlifts barely work biceps, calves or forearms, so there is no excuse
With damaged elbows, one regular pushdown variation plus heavy presses is enough for triceps, but still include a long-head movement; band extensions are good
Hack squats are good for hypertrophy, with big range of motion and less lower back strain, and could even replace back squats, though variations are hard to find and you can still get hurt
Hack squats plus lunges or reverse lunges will build really big legs
Zerchers make a good variation but not a main squat unless you are an athlete such as a wrestler; Zercher squats and deadlifts need lower back rigidity and core strength novices lack
Front squats as the main quad lift only make sense for Olympic weightlifters or people who love them
He trains legs three times a week with a heavy hip hinge or knee flexion every two days; you could train them four times a week for big legs

For big delts do three or four heavy presses a week (two vertical and two horizontal, or three vertical and one horizontal) plus lighter, higher-rep lateral and rear delt work, up to four or five days a week while watching shoulder health
To prioritise legs and delts, upper/lower three times each with lateral raises on lower days beats PPL; full body works but is hard to schedule around heavy leg lifts
Comparing your progress to others either disgusts you with the sport or lowers your standards and kills your drive
For pain between chest and shoulder after benching he used a Slingshot, then pause, Spoto and close-grip bench, and never returned to heavy touch-and-go bench
If push-ups do not hurt, switch to weighted push-ups; massaging and obsessing over the pain keeps it around
With long legs and duck feet, high bar is probably out; do goblet squats two to three times a week to learn to let the knees travel forward, since forcing knees out causes lower back injuries
If squats do not suit your build, lunges, reverse lunges and goblet squats can still build good legs
He trains comfortably at 100 F with high humidity as long as he drinks water between sets
In the heat, gulp water between sets, blast a fan in your face, acclimatise by skipping AC and sleeping warm after a cold shower, and eat salt for electrolytes
mTOR resets and breaks to resensitise muscle are a powerlifting principle repackaged; muscle is never desensitised, and evolving rep ranges and rotations already handle accumulated fatigue
Sauna is likely good for health by forcing adaptation, like cold showers; its effect on growth is unknown and you should watch your heart
He avoids big shoulders so they do not overpower the arms, is now cutting shoulder tonnage because they are getting too big, does not care about upper chest, and goes overboard on legs
Novices can grow everything, but advanced lifters must make aesthetic sacrifices in some areas to reach their goal physique
Train for the physique you want even if it does not match the mainstream
His tendinitis turned into non-permanent tendon damage because he lifted too heavy and ignored the pain
30 sets of push-ups and pull-ups can work, but harder or weighted variations give similar results in much less time
Brachialis growth makes the arm look wider and more 3D from the front; six sets of hammer curls a week costs nothing
Beginners do better with one knee flexion and one hip hinge variation per day than three lower-body lifts
Avoid squats followed by snatch-grip deadlifts; open with the snatch-grip deadlift then do a pause squat; he also dislikes straight squat and deadlift on the same day
Deadlift followed by front squat works because front squats load the lumbar spine less; an RDL after is fine in higher reps with controlled range
Front squats took him about two years to get comfortable with; learn the rack position from Olympic weightlifting videos
The fridge physique comes from building the torso at the expense of arms and legs; avoid only doing the big three plus chin-ups, isolate the arms and do not overbulk
For serratus, do pullovers, Russian twists and core bracing; his rib-rehab serratus punches gave him definition there
Damaging the baseline is the best sign of growth; failing reps on later sets of 3x5 means the top set did its job
Dropping the weight 10% when you miss 3x5 throws away high-quality tonnage; a 5,4,3 is an evolving rep range to embrace, moving to 5,4,3 with more weight once you hit 5,5,5
Vary rep ranges across your program and make every day a mix of light and heavy work
Belt squats carry over to the squat, better to high bar because of the upright torso, with little lower back impact; they will lead to bigger legs for many people
Of the machines he liked the cable row for upper back and the triceps pulley; machines are good but often cannot replace free weights
After about six months start building your own programs instead of depending on others, but you can stay a novice for strength up to two years and should not hop between programs

He does no heavy strength work for the upper back: heavy rows are hip hinge hybrids, and he avoids weighted chins to protect his wooden platform, using grease-the-groove chin-ups with ankle weights instead
The upper back handles a lot of volume, so it works better as a secondary focus spread across every day than as the heavy anchor of one day
exercises: use a band instead of loaded barbell
gives full range while heavy squats stop at parallel
be careful, still possible to get hurt
big range of motion, less lower back strain
need lower back rigidity and core strength
teaches squat pattern for long-legged lifters
alternative to bench for cranky shoulders
quad work with little lower back load
do before squat variations, not after
reduces injury risk from lower back fatigue
weighted upper back work without risking the platform
